newsitem.title: USA: ASARCO voices concern about Sumitomo's role.
newsitem.headline: ASARCO voices concern about Sumitomo's role.

text.p: Disinformation spread by copper market participants and the lack of candor by Sumitomo Corp over its positions in the market have damaged the metal's health, Richard de J Osborne, ASARCO's chairman said.

In response to the Sumitomo affair, Osborne has written to the U.K. regulatory watchdog, the Securities and Investments Board, to suggest that users of the LME should face the same disclosure requirements the U.S. Securities and Exchanges Commission imposes.
"If Sumitomo was SEC registered, they would have had to be very much more explicit about what their positions are. I have written to the SIB with exactly that point of view in mind."

Osborne said the LME itself had performed well and that the onus should be on individual participants on the London exchange to disclose information about positions "or suffer the consequences if they do not."
It was not up to the LME to disclose such information on any participant's behalf, Osborne added.
"Having said that, the uncertainty created by Sumitomo has given traders and particularly short sellers opportunities to use this uncertainty."
Osborne said the market has "witnessed some very public displays of public relations" on the part of those who have been quiet in the past.
"I tend to believe the opposite of what these people say," Osborne said.
When questioned by reporters later, Osborne declined to specify any particular market participant he had in mind.
"The market would be far more orderly if the world knew about Sumitomo's position. We would not still be reading about 1.5 million tonnes of hidden hoards of copper," Osborne said.
The letter to the SIB was a voluntary gesture and was not requested as part of the watchdog's ongoing probe into the copper market and the LME's workings, Osborne added.

Osborne said he had no deep knowledge of the British regulatory system, but from those who had that he had spoken to, it seemed the likelihood was that only minor changes would come about following the SIB's probes.

Regarding what he saw as the spread of disinformation in the copper market, Osborne told reporters after the briefing that market participants should "not be in a position to fabricate stories that they may have no direct knowledge of."
Osborne noted that copper stocks have dropped like a rock along with prices. "I have never seen a market where the underlying fundamentals are so strong, but the prices have been so weak."
Osborne said such a development was counter intuitive and non-economic. "Something is going on," he added.
